Deep Randomized Distributed Function Computation (DeepRDFC):
Neural Distributed Channel Simulation
Didrik Bergström and Onur Günlü
Information Theory and Security Laboratory (ITSL), Linköping University, Sweden
Email: {didrik.bergstrom, onur.gunlu}@liu.se
Abstract—The randomized distributed function computation
(RDFC) framework, which unifies many cutting-edge distributed
computation and learning applications, is considered. An au-
toencoder (AE) architecture is proposed to minimize the total
variation distance between the probability distribution simulated
by the AE outputs and an unknown target distribution, using only
data samples. We illustrate significantly high RDFC performance
with communication load gains from our AEs compared to data
compression methods. Our designs establish deep learning-based
RDFC methods and aim to facilitate the use of RDFC methods,
especially when the amount of common randomness is limited
and strong function computation guarantees are required.
I. INTRODUCTION
In conventional systems, data is communicated as arbitrary
bit sequences without considering the conveyed meaning. This
deficiency has motivatedsemantic communications[1], [2],
where the quality measure of transmission depends on the
semantics [3]. For example, transmitting objects and their
relative positions, rather than raw pixel arrays, exemplifies
semantic communication [3]. As the semantics of data can be
modeled as a function of the data, the semantic communication
paradigm can be defined as a remote (hidden) source coding
problem where the transmitted information is a function of
the data, while the function output is not available to the
transmitter [4, pp. 78], [5, pp. 118], [6]. This formulation
extends beyond classical lossy coding by employing semantic-
driven fidelity metrics [7]–[9].
We consider a generalization of remote source coding that
employs arandomizedfunctional mapping for distributed
function computation. In this setting, the receiver’s compu-
tation relies on randomized transformations of the transmit-
ter’s data, thus defining arandomized distributed function
computation (RDFC)framework, introduced in [7]. RDFC
unifies a large set of important problems that leverage se-
mantic communications. Example RDFC applications include
machine learning-based data compression methods with gen-
erative models [10], [11], federated learning (FL) with side
information [12], transform coding methods [13], [14], lossy
compression methods with realism constraints (such as visual
perception) [15], [16], and compression methods used as
differential privacy mechanisms [17], [18]. These applications
aim to synthesize data according to a target joint proba-
bility distribution, which broadly corresponds to controlling
the correlation between data samples to satisfy a constraint
requiring a controlled randomization step. Minimizing thecommunication load required for RDFC is defined as acoor-
dination problem[19]–[22], also known as distributed channel
simulation/synthesis.
We focus on strong coordination [19], imposing joint
typicality constraints on each function computation. Such a
stringent constraint is vital to ensure a performance guaran-
tee for each computation instance, unlike previous methods
whose guarantee is for the average case over all computation
instances, where the latter provides empirical coordination.
Moreover, unlike computations of deterministic functions,
common randomness shared between transmitter and receiver
can significantly reduce the communication load for RDFC
[23]. Such uniformly distributed common randomness can be
obtained, e.g., by using physical unclonable functions [24]. For
instance, if encoder-decoder pairs that apply RDFC methods
are used to achieve local differential privacy, the communica-
tion load is reduced by up to 214 times compared to adding
noise for the same purpose [7]. Thus, in this work, we propose
deep learning methods to design low-complexity encoder-
decoder pairs for the RDFC framework. There are a few code
constructions proposed for empirical coordination problems,
such as in [25], designed for binary symmetric channels
(BSCs), and existential designs for strong coordination, such
as in [26]. These existing designs do not provide constructive
code designs for RDFC and do not leverage the high perfor-
mance of deep neural networks, illustrated to surpass classical
code constructions for reliable communications [27].
Our summary of the main contributions is as follows:
•We develop a general constructive design of autoencoders
(AEs) for RDFC in a discrete setting. We propose a suit-
able loss function for RDFC and algorithms to generate
training data that provide high RDFC performance.
•We provide an AE architecture and technical insights to
facilitate the training and application of AEs in RDFC.
We motivate our choices of layer activation functions,
training parameters, and the need for a vector quantizer
layer that determines the RDFC rate for our setting.
•We demonstrate the feasibility of our design by simulat-
ing a BSC in a distributed computation setting. We also
illustrate the impact of the amount of available common
randomness on the RDFC performance.

A. Loss Function for TVD Minimization
Using TVD as the loss function is intractable in this
setting because the gradient descent tends to get stuck in
local minima. Therefore, we use CCE as our loss function
during the training phase. CCE is a suitable surrogate loss
function to TVD due to (i) its differentiability and (ii) its
equivalence to Kullback-Liebler divergence if the AE’s inputs
and outputs are one-hot encoded, which is the case in our
design. Moreover, Kullback-Liebler divergence bounds TVD
from above via Pinsker’s inequality [30].

V. CONCLUSION
We proposed AE designs for the RDFC framework, pro-
viding significant communication load gains for multiple dis-
tributed computation and learning problems. We demonstrated
that our AE designs achieve high RDFC performance for
distributed synthesis of a BSC, where the amount of common
randomness was shown to play a crucial role. Furthermore,
we provided fundamental information-theoretic insights into
the network architecture and the training-data generation.
With this work, we aimed to facilitate the use of RDFC
techniques for cutting-edge use cases, including neural image
compression, FL with side information, and distributed secure
and private function computation. Finally, while one can show
that there is a gap between the achieved rate tuples and the
asymptotic RDFC limits, such a comparison does not provide
meaningful insights due to the short blocklengths considered
in this work. Thus, in future work, we will apply, for example,
hybrid coding methods introduced in [34] to our AE designs
to consider practical blocklengths.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
The document introduces Deep Randomized Distributed Function Computation (DeepRDFC), a framework that unifies various distributed computation and learning applications. The core of the proposal is an autoencoder (AE) architecture designed to minimize the total variation distance between a simulated probability distribution and an unknown target distribution, using only data samples. The authors highlight significant performance gains in terms of communication load compared to traditional data compression methods. The work aims to facilitate the use of RDFC, particularly in scenarios with limited common randomness and a need for strong function computation guarantees.

The document also touches upon semantic communications, defining it as a remote source coding problem where the transmitted information is a function of the data, with the function output unknown to the transmitter. RDFC is presented as a generalization of this concept, employing randomized functional mappings for distributed computation. Examples of RDFC applications include machine learning-based data compression, federated learning, transform coding, and differential privacy mechanisms.

A key focus is on "strong coordination," which ensures performance guarantees for each computation instance, contrasting with previous methods that offered average-case guarantees. The paper emphasizes that shared common randomness can substantially reduce communication load in RDFC. The authors propose deep learning-based methods to design low-complexity encoder-decoder pairs for RDFC, noting that existing code constructions lack constructiveness and do not leverage the performance of deep neural networks.

The main contributions are summarized as:
*   A general constructive design of autoencoders for RDFC in a discrete setting, including a suitable loss function and algorithms for generating training data.
*   An AE architecture with technical insights on layer activation functions, training parameters, and the necessity of a vector quantizer layer for determining the RDFC rate.
*   Demonstration of the design's feasibility through simulations on a Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) and analysis of the impact of common randomness on RDFC performance.

The document also provides notation definitions and outlines the structure of the paper, with Section II introducing the RDFC framework and reviewing AEs, Section III detailing the AE-based RDFC design, Section IV presenting experimental results, and Section V offering conclusions. The system model for distributed channel simulation is described, involving an encoder and decoder that utilize source input, common randomness, and local randomness to synthesize a target joint probability distribution. The RDFC rate region is defined and discussed in relation to the amount of common randomness.

nodes.title: Review of AEs
nodes.summary:
The document discusses a framework called RDFC (Rate-Distortion Function for Channels) and proposes using Autoencoders (AEs) to implement it. The core problem is distributed channel simulation, where an encoder-decoder pair aims to synthesize a target probability distribution $Q_{\bar{X}\bar{Y}}$ using source input $\bar{X}$, common randomness $\bar{K}$, and local randomness $\bar{L}$.

Key points covered include:

*   **Definitions:** The document defines various mathematical concepts like binning sets, Markov chains, total variation distance (TVD), $\ell_2$ norm, categorical cross-entropy (CCE) loss function, Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC), and uniform distributions.
*   **RDFC Framework:** It introduces the RDFC framework and its rate region, which defines achievable rate triples $(R, R_0, R_L)$ for synthesizing a target distribution. The system model for distributed channel simulation is presented, showing how an encoder-decoder pair generates output $\bar{Y}$ based on inputs $\bar{X}$, $\bar{K}$, and $\bar{L}$.
*   **Autoencoders (AEs):** A review of AEs is provided, explaining their encoder-decoder structure and training process using loss functions and gradient descent. In this context, the AE takes source input and randomness as inputs and outputs the synthesized channel output.
*   **AE-based RDFC:** The document proposes AEs designed for the RDFC framework. It details algorithms for generating training data (Algorithm 1 and 2) which involve binning of randomness variables to match target probabilities.
*   **Loss Function:** It explains the choice of Categorical Cross-Entropy (CCE) as a surrogate loss function for minimizing TVD during AE training, due to its differentiability and relationship with Kullback-Leibler divergence.
*   **Experimental Setup:** The document outlines the general layout of the AE architecture (Table I) and mentions that experimental results will be presented and discussed in a later section.

structure.title: AE-BASEDRDFC
structure.summary:
The document describes a method for training an Autoencoder (AE) for a task involving synthesized joint distributions. The core of the approach lies in constructing a training dataset that effectively captures the relationships between inputs ($\bar{X}$, $\bar{K}$, $\bar{L}$) and outputs ($\bar{Y}$).

The main points covered are:

*   **AE Formulation:** An AE is denoted as $P_\theta(\bar{Y}|\bar{X}, \bar{K}, \bar{L})$, where $\theta$ represents network parameters. The synthesized joint distribution is defined as $P_{\bar{X}\bar{Y}}(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \sum_{\bar{k},\bar{l}} P_{\bar{X}}(\bar{x}) \cdot P_\theta(\bar{Y}|\bar{X}, \bar{K}, \bar{L})(\bar{y}|\bar{x}, \bar{k}, \bar{l}) \cdot U_{\bar{K}} \cdot U_{\bar{L}}$.
*   **Training Set Construction:** The performance of the AE is highly dependent on the training data. Two algorithms are presented for constructing this training set:
    *   **Algorithm 1 (Binning of K and L):** This algorithm partitions the output space $\bar{Y}$ into bins of width $\beta$ (output bins $B(\bar{y})$). For each input $\bar{x}$, it then determines bins for common randomness $\bar{K}$ ($B(\bar{k})(\bar{x})$) and local randomness $\bar{L}$ ($B(\bar{l})(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$). These bins are constructed based on estimated conditional probabilities to ensure that the training data covers the relevant input-output relationships.
    *   **Algorithm 2 (Training Data Generation):** This algorithm takes the samples from the target distribution $Q_{\bar{X}\bar{Y}}$ and the bins generated by Algorithm 1. It then samples realizations of $\bar{K}$ and $\bar{L}$ uniformly from the corresponding bins for each sample $(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_i)$, creating the complete training set $\{ \bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_i, \bar{k}_i, \bar{l}_i \}$.
*   **AE Implementation Details:**
    *   The AE uses one-hot encoded input-output vectors and a softmax activation function in the output layer to predict the most likely output.
    *   Common randomness $\bar{K}$ and local randomness $\bar{L}$ are encoded as binary sequences.
    *   The AE architecture is described in Table I, detailing the layers, input/output dimensions, and activation functions.
    *   Inference involves rounding the output using argmax for hard decisions.
*   **Loss Function:**
    *   Minimizing Total Variation Distance (TVD) directly is intractable.
    *   Cross-Entropy Loss (CCE) is used as a surrogate loss function during training due to its differentiability and equivalence to Kullback-Liebler divergence for one-hot encoded inputs/outputs.
    *   Pinsker's inequality is mentioned as bounding TVD from above by KL divergence.

It also describes how training data is constructed from a target joint distribution and how the AE is trained for a fixed number of epochs.
*   **Testing Procedure:** Outlines the creation of a separate test set, the computation of an estimated joint distribution for testing, and how the AE's predictions are used to synthesize a joint distribution. The evaluation metric is the total variation distance (TVD) between the synthesized and ground-truth distributions.
*   **Vector Quantizer Layer:** Explains the implementation of a vector quantizer (VQ) layer used to constrain the RDFC rate. It details how the VQ layer selects the closest discrete index from an embedding space and the use of a straight-through estimator for gradient propagation.
*   **Experimental Setup and Results:** Describes the experimental setup using a Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) as the target distribution, with binary inputs and outputs, and uniformly random common and local randomness. It presents results in Table II, comparing scenarios with only local randomness (LR-cases) versus those with both common and local randomness (LR+CR-cases). The results indicate that LR+CR-cases generally achieve better RDFC performance, and increasing local randomness also improves performance, especially for higher crossover probabilities.

It also touches upon the role of allowing empty sets in certain conditional probabilities for improved RDFC performance.

nodes.title: A. AE Design Insights
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the design of autoencoders (AEs) for the Randomized Distributed Function Computation (RDFC) framework, highlighting their benefits for distributed computation and learning. Key findings include:

*   **Activation Function and Quantization:** The sigmoid activation function in layer 7 leads to faster training convergence and lower quantization error compared to ReLU, likely due to normalization aligning encoder outputs with the latent alphabet.
*   **Network Depth:** Deeper encoders and decoders converge faster than shallower ones for a fixed network width, though the exact reason (more parameters vs. inherent depth advantage) is not definitively determined.
*   **RDFC Performance:** Allowing empty sets in the conditional probability distribution B(l)(x, y) can improve RDFC performance, but the impact of allowing empty sets in B(k)(x) is dependent on the specific channel characteristics (Q Y|X) and sample size (n).
*   **Conclusion:** The work proposes AE designs for RDFC, demonstrating significant communication gains in distributed synthesis of a Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC). The importance of common randomness is emphasized. The paper also provides theoretical insights into network architecture and data generation, aiming to facilitate RDFC applications in areas like neural image compression, federated learning, and secure distributed computation. Future work will explore hybrid coding methods for practical blocklengths.
*   **Visualizations:** Figure 2 presents heatmaps illustrating conditional probability distributions (Q X,Y and P X,Y) for a BSC, showing how different configurations affect these distributions.
